etymology: Greek Gadara; the city of the Gadarenes, one of the cities of the Decapolis east of the Sea of Galilee. The region is variously called the country of the Gadarenes, Gergesenes, or Gerasenes in the Gospel accounts.
biblical_def: Gadara was a city of the Decapolis east of the Sea of Galilee, in whose region the Lord Jesus healed the demon-possessed man (or men) and permitted the legion of demons to enter a herd of swine that rushed into the sea. The Gospels (Matt 8:28-34; Mark 5:1-20; Luke 8:26-39) record that as the Lord came to the country of the Gadarenes, He was met by a man (Matthew mentions two) possessed by an unclean spirit of terrible power, who dwelt among the tombs, broke every chain, and cried out night and day, cutting himself with stones. The Lord asked the spirit's name; it answered, "My name is Legion: for we are many" (Mark 5:9). The demons begged not to be sent into the deep but into a nearby herd of swine; the Lord permitted it, and the whole herd, about two thousand, ran violently down a steep place into the sea and drowned. The delivered man was found "sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind" (Luke 8:35). But the response of the people is the sobering point: when the townspeople saw the healed man and heard of the lost swine, "they began to pray him to depart out of their coasts" (Mark 5:17). They preferred their pigs to the Prince of life; they valued their property above the deliverance of a tormented soul, and they asked the Savior to leave. The Lord granted their request and departed — but He left behind the healed man as a missionary, commanding him to tell what great things the Lord had done for him, and the man published it through all the Decapolis (Mark 5:19-20). Gadara stands as a place of mighty deliverance and of tragic rejection: the demoniac was freed, but the region drove the Deliverer away, preferring swine to the Son of God. It is a searching picture of those who, faced with Christ's power, count the cost to their possessions and prefer their pigs to their Savior.

corruption_summary: Gadara is corrupted when the reality of demonic possession is dismissed, when the loss of the swine is read as the point rather than the people's preference of pigs to the Savior, or when the discrepancy among the Gospel place-names is treated as contradiction.
corruption_paragraphs: Possession-dismissed misreading. Modern naturalism dismisses the demon-possession at Gadara as a primitive misdiagnosis of mental illness. The Gospels present it as real and personal: the spirits spoke, named themselves Legion, begged the Lord, entered the swine, and drove them to destruction — events no theory of mental illness explains. The Lord Jesus dealt with demons as real, malevolent, personal beings under His sovereign authority, and the deliverance was a real exorcism, not a psychological cure. The dictionary holds with Scripture that the demonic is real, that Christ has absolute authority over it, and that the Gadara account is sober history, not folklore.

Pigs-over-Savior point missed. The heart of the Gadara narrative is not the loss of the swine but the response of the people: they saw a man delivered from a legion of demons, restored to his right mind, and their reaction was to beg the Lord to leave — because the deliverance had cost them their pigs. They valued their property above a saved soul and their economy above the Son of God. It is one of the most searching pictures in the Gospels of the human heart that counts the cost of Christ to its possessions and finds the Savior too expensive. Many still prefer their pigs to their Savior, asking the Lord who threatens their idols to depart out of their coasts.

etymology: Greek Antiocheia; the great city on the Orontes River in Syria, capital of the Roman province of Syria, founded by Seleucus I and named for his father Antiochus. Distinct from Antioch of Pisidia in Asia Minor.
biblical_def: Antioch in Syria was the third-greatest city of the Roman Empire (after Rome and Alexandria) and the cradle of Gentile Christianity and of the worldwide missionary movement — the church from which Paul and Barnabas were sent out and the place where the disciples were first called Christians. After the persecution that arose over Stephen scattered the believers, some came to Antioch and preached the gospel not only to Jews but to Greeks (Gentiles), "and the hand of the Lord was with them: and a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord" (Acts 11:21). The Jerusalem church sent Barnabas to investigate; seeing the grace of God, he rejoiced, and fetched Saul (Paul) from Tarsus to help teach the growing church. "And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch" (Acts 11:26) — the name "Christian" ("those of Christ") was coined there, marking the new community as a distinct people defined by their Lord. Antioch became the model of a Gentile-inclusive, gospel-centered, mission-minded church. It was there, as the prophets and teachers ministered to the Lord and fasted, that the Holy Spirit said, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them" (Acts 13:2), launching the first missionary journey. Antioch was the sending church, the base to which Paul returned to report (Acts 14:26-27), and the church at the center of the controversy over Gentile circumcision that led to the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15). Antioch thus stands as the prototype of the missionary church: a congregation of Jews and Gentiles together, taught the Word, worshipping and fasting, sensitive to the Spirit, and sending its best men out to the nations. Where Jerusalem was the mother church of the Jewish believers, Antioch became the mother church of the Gentile mission — the launching point of the gospel to the ends of the earth.

corruption_summary: Antioch is corrupted when its role as the launching church of missions is forgotten, when the name "Christian" is severed from its Antiochene origin as a marker of belonging to Christ, or when the Gentile-inclusive, Spirit-sent model it provides is neglected.
corruption_paragraphs: Missionary-model neglected. Antioch is the New Testament's prototype of the missionary church, and its features are instructive: a congregation of Jews and Gentiles together, taught the Word for a whole year, worshipping and fasting before the Lord, sensitive to the leading of the Spirit, and willing to send out its very best men (Barnabas and Saul, its chief teachers) to the unreached nations. The modern church that wishes to recover a missionary heart should look to Antioch: missions arose not from a committee or a program but from a worshipping, Word-saturated, Spirit-sensitive church that gave its best to the Great Commission. The door of faith was opened to the Gentiles (Acts 14:27) through a church that fasted, prayed, and sent.

Antioch has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the origin and meaning of the name "Christian." It was at Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26) — a name meaning "those belonging to Christ," marking the new community as a distinct people defined not by ethnicity, law, or nation but by their Lord. The name, possibly first given by outsiders, captured the truth: these were Christ's people. To wear the name "Christian" is to confess belonging to Christ; it was born at Antioch, the church where Jew and Gentile were one in Him and the gospel went out to the world.

etymology: Greek Lystra; a city in the region of Lycaonia in Asia Minor (modern Turkey), visited by Paul on his first missionary journey. The hometown of Timothy.
biblical_def: Lystra was a city in Lycaonia in Asia Minor where the Apostle Paul, on his first missionary journey, healed a man crippled from birth, was hailed as a god by the pagan crowd, and then, when the crowd turned, was stoned and left for dead — and which was the hometown of his beloved disciple Timothy. When Paul preached at Lystra, he saw a man who had never walked and, perceiving his faith, commanded him to stand; the man leaped and walked (Acts 14:8-10). The pagan people of Lystra, astonished, cried out in their own language that "the gods are come down to us in the likeness of men," and called Barnabas Jupiter (Zeus) and Paul Mercurius (Hermes), and the priest of Jupiter prepared to offer sacrifice to them (Acts 14:11-13). Paul and Barnabas, horrified, rent their clothes and ran among the people, crying, "Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God" (Acts 14:15) — a model of how God's servants refuse worship and turn all glory to God. But the fickle crowd was soon turned by hostile Jews from Antioch and Iconium; they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing him dead. As the disciples stood round him, he rose up and went back into the city (Acts 14:19-20) — a striking testimony to God's preserving power and Paul's undaunted courage. Lystra teaches several lessons: the danger of misdirected worship (the crowd ready to worship men), the duty of God's servants to refuse all glory and point men to the living God, the fickleness of crowd-approval (worshipping one day, stoning the next), and the perseverance of the gospel through suffering. And Lystra gave the church Timothy, "well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium" (Acts 16:1-2), Paul's son in the faith and fellow-laborer.

corruption_summary: Lystra is corrupted when the lesson of refused worship is overlooked, when the fickleness of crowd-approval is missed, or when the stoning of Paul is read apart from the perseverance of the gospel through suffering.
corruption_paragraphs: Refused-worship lesson missed. When the crowd at Lystra prepared to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods, the apostles' response is a model for every servant of God who is tempted to receive glory: they rent their clothes in horror, ran among the people, and cried, "We also are men of like passions with you" (Acts 14:15), turning all worship to the living God. In an age that builds platforms and cults of personality even within the church, the apostles' refusal of worship is a sharp rebuke. The true servant of God deflects all glory to God and refuses to let men make idols of him; he insists, "We are men like you" and points beyond himself to Christ.

Lystra has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the fickleness of crowd-approval and the perseverance of the gospel through suffering. The same crowd that one moment hailed Paul as a god, the next moment stoned him and left him for dead — a sober warning against trusting the praise of crowds, which turns as quickly to violence (as Jerusalem's "Hosanna" turned to "Crucify"). And Paul's rising from the stoning to walk back into the very city that had stoned him testifies to God's preserving power and the undaunted courage of the gospel, which presses on through suffering to plant the church — the church that would give the world Timothy.

etymology: Greek Derbē; a city in the region of Lycaonia in Asia Minor, the easternmost point of Paul's first missionary journey. The hometown of Gaius, one of Paul's companions.
biblical_def: Derbe was a city in Lycaonia in Asia Minor, the farthest point reached on Paul's first missionary journey, and a place of fruitful and relatively peaceful gospel labor in contrast to the violence Paul had just suffered at nearby Lystra. After being stoned and left for dead at Lystra, Paul rose and, with Barnabas, "departed unto Derbe. And when they had preached the gospel to that city, and had taught many, they returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and Antioch" (Acts 14:20-21). At Derbe the apostles "taught many" and "made many disciples" (the Greek of v. 21 suggests a significant ingathering) without the recorded opposition that marked the other cities of the journey — a reminder that the gospel meets varied responses in different places, and that seasons of fierce persecution may be followed by seasons of fruitful peace. From Derbe, the eastern limit of the journey, Paul and Barnabas turned back the way they had come, retracing their steps through the very cities where they had been persecuted, "confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22), and ordaining elders in every church (Acts 14:23). This pattern — not merely making converts but returning to strengthen, organize, and warn them of the tribulation ahead — is a model of apostolic care for the churches. Derbe was also the hometown of Gaius, one of the companions who later accompanied Paul as a delegate of the relief collection (Acts 20:4). Derbe stands as a quiet but important place: the turning-point of the first missionary journey, a city of fruitful labor and many disciples, from which the apostles returned to strengthen the young churches in the faith.

corruption_summary: Derbe is corrupted only when its quiet fruitfulness is overlooked, when the apostolic pattern of returning to strengthen converts is neglected, or when the warning that we must through much tribulation enter the kingdom is softened.
corruption_paragraphs: Strengthen-the-converts pattern neglected. Derbe marks the turning-point where Paul and Barnabas, having reached the farthest city, turned back to retrace their steps through the very towns where they had been persecuted — not to make new converts but to strengthen the ones already made: "confirming the souls of the disciples... and ordaining elders in every church" (Acts 14:22-23). This is a vital and often-neglected pattern of apostolic care: evangelism that does not stop at conversion but returns to establish, organize, and shepherd the converts. The church that makes disciples but does not strengthen and order them has done half the work. From Derbe, Paul models the fuller pattern: confirm the souls, ordain the elders, warn of the tribulation, commend them to the Lord.

Derbe has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the apostolic word spoken on the return from Derbe: "we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22). Paul, freshly risen from a stoning, did not promise the new disciples ease, prosperity, or the world's favor; he warned them that the path to the kingdom runs through much tribulation. This is the honest gospel, against the prosperity teaching that promises health and wealth: the kingdom is entered through tribulation, the cross precedes the crown, and the disciple who would follow Christ must take up his cross. The strengthening Paul gave was not comfort that flatters but truth that prepares for suffering.

etymology: Aramaic Chaqal Dema ("field of blood"), transliterated into Greek as Akeldama (Acts 1:19). The field bought with the thirty pieces of silver Judas received for betraying Christ.
biblical_def: Aceldama ("the field of blood") was a field near Jerusalem associated with the thirty pieces of silver that Judas Iscariot received for betraying the Lord Jesus, and with Judas's own terrible end. The Gospels and Acts give complementary accounts. Matthew records that Judas, seized with remorse, brought the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests, confessing, "I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood"; they would not take it back, and Judas cast down the silver in the temple and went and hanged himself. The chief priests, unwilling to put the "price of blood" into the treasury, took the money and bought with it the potter's field to bury strangers in, "wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day" (Matt 27:3-8) — and Matthew sees in this a fulfillment of prophecy (Zech 11:12-13; Jer 32). Acts adds that Judas "purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out... and it was called... Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood" (Acts 1:18-19). The two accounts harmonize: the priests bought the field with Judas's blood-money (so it was "his" purchase, the fruit of his iniquity), and Judas hanged himself, his body afterward falling and bursting open. Aceldama stands as a permanent monument to the wages of betrayal: the field bought with the price of innocent blood, the burial-ground for strangers, named forever "the field of blood." It is bound up with the doom of Judas, "the son of perdition" (John 17:12), who betrayed the Lord with a kiss for thirty pieces of silver (the price of a slave, Exod 21:32), and who went "to his own place" (Acts 1:25). Aceldama testifies that the price of betraying Christ is blood and ruin, and that the silver of treachery purchases only a grave.

corruption_summary: Aceldama is corrupted when the Matthew and Acts accounts are alleged to contradict, when Judas's remorse is mistaken for saving repentance, or when the monument to the wages of betrayal is read as mere grim history.
corruption_paragraphs: Contradiction-alleged misreading. Skeptics claim Matthew (Judas hanged himself; the priests bought the field) and Acts (Judas bought the field; he fell and burst open) contradict each other. They harmonize naturally: the priests purchased the field with Judas's blood-money, so it was in effect "his" purchase, the fruit of his iniquity (Acts speaks of what his money did); and Judas hanged himself (Matthew), his body afterward falling, perhaps when the rope or branch broke, and bursting open on the ground (Acts describes the aftermath). The two accounts are complementary, not contradictory — one describing the means (hanging) and the other the gruesome result (the fall and bursting), one the priests' purchase and the other its source in Judas's money.

Remorse-mistaken-for-repentance misreading. Judas "repented himself" (Matt 27:3) and confessed, "I have betrayed the innocent blood" — yet he is the son of perdition who went to his own place (Acts 1:25). His remorse was not saving repentance. The Greek word for his "repentance" (metamelētheis, regret) differs from the saving repentance (metanoia) that turns to Christ for mercy. Judas felt the horror of his sin and the weight of his guilt, but he turned not to the Savior he had betrayed but to despair and self-destruction. This is the difference between worldly sorrow, which "worketh death," and godly sorrow, which "worketh repentance to salvation" (2 Cor 7:10). Judas's remorse drove him to a noose; true repentance would have driven him to the very Christ he had betrayed, who receives even the chief of sinners. Aceldama is a warning: remorse without turning to Christ ends in ruin.

etymology: Latin praetorium, the official residence or headquarters of a Roman governor or commander; the judgment hall. Greek praitōrion. The place where the Lord Jesus was tried before Pilate and mocked by the soldiers.
biblical_def: The Praetorium was the official residence and judgment hall of the Roman governor — in the Gospels, the place in Jerusalem where the Lord Jesus was brought before Pontius Pilate, tried, condemned, and mocked by the Roman soldiers. The term (Latin praetorium) denoted the headquarters of a Roman commander or the governor's official quarters; in the passion narratives it is the seat of Roman judgment where the Lord was delivered after the Jewish trial. It was to the Praetorium that the chief priests led Jesus from Caiaphas early in the morning; significantly, "they themselves went not into the judgment hall, lest they should be defiled; but that they might eat the passover" (John 18:28) — a stark irony, that they scrupled over ceremonial defilement while plotting the murder of the Son of God. Within the Praetorium, Pilate examined Jesus, found no fault in Him, and yet, fearing the crowd, delivered Him to be scourged and crucified. There the soldiers of the governor took Jesus and gathered the whole band; they stripped Him and put on Him a scarlet robe, plaited a crown of thorns and pressed it on His head, put a reed in His right hand, bowed the knee in mockery, crying, "Hail, King of the Jews!", spat on Him, and smote Him (Matt 27:27-31; Mark 15:16-20; John 19:1-3). The Praetorium thus became the scene of the most profound mockery in history: the King of kings crowned with thorns and hailed in derision by the soldiers of an earthly power, the Lord of glory enduring the spitting and smiting of His creatures. Paul later writes from his own imprisonment that his bonds in Christ were "manifest in all the palace" (the praetorium, the imperial guard, Phil 1:13), so that the gospel penetrated even the praetorian guard at Rome. The Praetorium stands as the place where earthly justice failed utterly — condemning the innocent to please the crowd — and where the Lord, mocked as a false king, was in truth the true King, reigning from the very humiliation His enemies heaped upon Him.

corruption_summary: The Praetorium is corrupted when the mockery of Christ is read as mere historical cruelty rather than the King reigning through humiliation, when Pilate's injustice is excused, or when the irony of the priests' ceremonial scruple is missed.
corruption_paragraphs: King-through-humiliation missed. The mockery in the Praetorium — the crown of thorns, the scarlet robe, the reed, the bowing knee, the cry "Hail, King of the Jews" — was intended by the soldiers as derision: here was a pretender to kingship, fit only for ridicule. But the Gospels intend the reader to see the deeper truth: the One they mocked as a false king was in truth the true King, and He was even then reigning — not in spite of the humiliation but through it, by the very suffering by which He would purchase His kingdom. The crown of thorns, emblem of the curse (Gen 3:18), He wore to bear the curse; the title "King of the Jews," meant in mockery, Pilate fixed to the cross in truth (John 19:19-22). The Praetorium displays the paradox of the gospel: the King crowned with thorns, reigning from His humiliation.

The Praetorium has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the failure of earthly justice and the sovereignty of God over it. Pilate, the Roman judge, found no fault in Jesus (John 18:38; 19:4, 6), declared Him innocent — and yet, to please the crowd and protect himself, condemned the innocent to death. It is the supreme miscarriage of justice in history: the only sinless man condemned by the law's own representative. Yet the Lord told Pilate, "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above" (John 19:11) — the injustice of the Praetorium was real and guilty, yet it accomplished the sovereign purpose of God, who delivered up His Son "by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God" (Acts 2:23). The Praetorium testifies both to the guilt of those who condemned the innocent and to the sovereignty of God who reigned over their injustice to redeem His people.

etymology: Aramaic/Hebrew Gabbatha ("elevated place, ridge"); Greek Lithostrōton ("the Pavement," a stone-paved area). The raised, paved place where Pilate sat in the judgment seat to pronounce sentence on the Lord Jesus (John 19:13).
biblical_def: Gabbatha ("the Pavement") was the raised, stone-paved place outside the Praetorium where Pontius Pilate sat in the judgment seat (the bēma) to pronounce his final sentence on the Lord Jesus. John alone records the detail: "When Pilate therefore heard that saying, he brought Jesus forth, and sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha" (John 19:13). The Greek name Lithostrōton means "stone-paved"; the Aramaic Gabbatha means "elevated place" or "ridge" — together describing a raised, paved platform where the Roman governor's tribunal was set. There Pilate, having failed to release Jesus and fearing the crowd's threat ("If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend," John 19:12), took his official seat to deliver the formal verdict. John fixes the time precisely: "it was the preparation of the passover, and about the sixth hour: and he saith unto the Jews, Behold your King!" (John 19:14). The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:15) — a stunning renunciation, the covenant nation declaring allegiance to the pagan emperor and rejecting their true King. Then Pilate delivered Jesus to be crucified. Gabbatha is thus the precise spot of the formal, legal condemnation of the Son of God — the place where the judgment seat of Rome pronounced the sentence that delivered the Innocent to the cross. The detail of the name, preserved by the eyewitness John, anchors the passion in real time and place. And it carries a solemn reversal: the One who stood condemned before Pilate's judgment seat at Gabbatha will Himself sit on the judgment seat before which all men, Pilate included, must stand (2 Cor 5:10; Acts 17:31). At Gabbatha the Judge of all the earth was judged, that those who believe in Him might not be condemned but pass from judgment to life.

corruption_summary: Gabbatha is corrupted when its precise eyewitness detail is dismissed, when the nation's cry "We have no king but Caesar" is softened, or when the reversal — the judged Christ becoming the Judge of all — is missed.
corruption_paragraphs: Eyewitness-detail dismissed. John's preservation of the place-name Gabbatha, with its Aramaic and Greek forms, is the mark of an eyewitness anchoring the events in real place and time ("the preparation of the passover, about the sixth hour"). Critics who treat the Gospels as late legend must reckon with such precise, incidental, untheological details, which bear the signature of memory, not invention. John was there; he saw Pilate ascend the raised Pavement and take his seat; he remembered the name in both tongues. The detail of Gabbatha is one of countless small testimonies to the historical reliability of the passion narratives, written by those who saw.

Gabbatha has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the nation's tragic renunciation and the great reversal. At Gabbatha, when Pilate presented their King, the chief priests cried, "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:15) — the covenant people, whose only true King was the LORD, renouncing Him for the pagan emperor, rejecting the Messiah they had awaited. And the deepest truth of Gabbatha is the reversal it foreshadows: the One who stood condemned before Pilate's judgment seat is the One before whose judgment seat all men, Pilate and the chief priests included, must one day stand (2 Cor 5:10; Acts 17:31). The Judge of all the earth was judged at Gabbatha, that those who believe might escape the judgment to come. The place of His condemnation is the ground of the believer's acquittal.

etymology: From Hebrew Shiloach ("sent"), Greek Silōam; a pool in Jerusalem fed by the waters of the Gihon spring through Hezekiah's tunnel. John notes its name means "Sent" (John 9:7).
biblical_def: The Pool of Siloam was a pool in Jerusalem, at the southern end of the City of David, fed by the Gihon spring through the tunnel King Hezekiah had cut through the rock (2 Kings 20:20); it is chiefly famous as the place where the Lord Jesus sent the man born blind to wash and receive his sight. In John 9, the Lord encountered a man blind from birth; rejecting the disciples' assumption that the blindness was punishment for someone's specific sin, He declared that it was "that the works of God should be made manifest in him" (John 9:3). He spat on the ground, made clay, anointed the blind man's eyes, and said, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam (which is by interpretation, Sent). He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing" (John 9:7). The healing led to one of the great chapters of confrontation in the Gospels: the healed man, interrogated by the Pharisees who refused to believe, grew bolder in his testimony until he confounded them — "Whereas I was blind, now I see" (John 9:25) — and was cast out of the synagogue, whereupon the Lord found him and revealed Himself as the Son of God, and the man worshipped Him. John's parenthetical note that "Siloam" means "Sent" is theologically pointed: the Lord Jesus is the Sent One, the one whom the Father sent (a theme throughout John's Gospel), so that the blind man washing in the pool called "Sent" pictures the cleansing and illumination that come through the Sent One, Christ Himself. The water of Siloam (also associated, in the Feast of Tabernacles, with the water-pouring ceremony at which the Lord cried, "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink," John 7:37) and the giving of sight to the blind together testify to Christ as the light of the world (John 9:5) and the giver of living water. The Pool of Siloam stands as a place where physical blindness was healed to display the deeper truth: that Christ the Sent One opens the eyes of the spiritually blind, and that those who come to Him, blind and helpless, go away seeing.

corruption_summary: The Pool of Siloam is corrupted when the healing is read as mere miracle without its meaning, when the name "Sent" is missed as pointing to Christ, or when the spiritual blindness the chapter exposes (in the seeing Pharisees) is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Name-meaning missed. John deliberately pauses to translate the name: the pool of Siloam means "Sent." This is no idle etymology. Throughout John's Gospel, the Lord Jesus is the Sent One, the one the Father sent into the world (John 3:17; 5:36-37; 17:18). The blind man washing in the pool named "Sent" to receive his sight is a living parable: cleansing and illumination come through the Sent One, Christ Himself. The man's physical sight, given through washing in "Sent," pictures the spiritual sight given to all who come to the Sent Savior. John's translation invites the reader to see the deeper meaning the water and the name carry.

The Pool of Siloam has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the contrast the chapter draws between the blind man who came to see and the seeing Pharisees who remained blind. The man born blind received both physical and spiritual sight, growing bolder in his confession until he worshipped Christ. The Pharisees, who had physical sight and religious learning, refused to see, and the Lord pronounced over them: "For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind... If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth" (John 9:39-41). The Pool of Siloam exposes the deeper blindness: the willful blindness of those who, claiming to see, reject the light of the world. The remedy for both blindnesses is the same — to come to Christ the Sent One, who gives sight to the blind and humbles the proud who think they see.

etymology: From Aramaic/Hebrew, possibly Beth-chesda ("house of mercy") or Beth-zatha; a pool in Jerusalem near the sheep market/gate, with five porches (John 5:2), where the Lord Jesus healed a man infirm for thirty-eight years.
biblical_def: The Pool of Bethesda (possibly "house of mercy") was a pool in Jerusalem near the sheep gate, surrounded by five porches, where a multitude of sick, blind, lame, and withered people lay, and where the Lord Jesus healed a man who had been infirm for thirty-eight years. John records: "Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches. In these lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered" (John 5:2-3). A man was there who had suffered his infirmity thirty-eight years — longer, perhaps, than many of those around him had been alive. The Lord saw him, knew his long-standing case, and asked the searching question, "Wilt thou be made whole?" (John 5:6). The man, fixated on the pool's waters and his inability to reach them in time, did not answer with faith but with his helplessness; yet the Lord, by sovereign grace, healed him with a word: "Rise, take up thy bed, and walk. And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked" (John 5:8-9). The healing took place on the Sabbath, provoking controversy with the Jewish leaders, who objected to the man carrying his bed; this led to the Lord's great discourse on His unity and equal working with the Father (John 5:17-47). The Pool of Bethesda teaches several lessons: the sovereignty of Christ's grace, which singled out one man from a multitude and healed him without his asking, on the ground of mercy alone (the "house of mercy" indeed); the helplessness of the sinner, pictured in the man who could not reach the healing waters by his own effort; and the power of Christ's word, which did in an instant what thirty-eight years of waiting by the pool could not do. The man's later warning from the Lord — "sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (John 5:14) — adds the sober note that physical healing is not the deepest need, and that the soul healed must turn from sin. Bethesda, the house of mercy, displays the mercy of Christ who heals the helpless by His sovereign word.

corruption_summary: The Pool of Bethesda is corrupted when the healing is read as a reward for the man's faith (which he did not show), when the "troubling of the water" tradition is over-weighted, or when the warning "sin no more" is severed from the healing.
corruption_paragraphs: Sovereign-mercy missed. The healing at Bethesda is a striking display of the sovereignty of Christ's grace. The Lord singled out one man from a great multitude of the sick — not the most faithful, not one who asked, not one who even knew who Jesus was (John 5:13) — and healed him on the ground of mercy alone. The man's response to "Wilt thou be made whole?" was not a confession of faith but a recital of his helplessness; yet Christ healed him anyway, by His own initiative and word. Bethesda ("house of mercy") thus pictures the gospel of sovereign grace: Christ heals the helpless sinner who cannot heal himself, choosing whom He will, on the ground of mercy, not the sinner's prior worthiness or even his asking. The thirty-eight years of failed effort by the pool could not do what Christ's word did in an instant.

The Pool of Bethesda has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering, beyond the sovereign mercy of the healing, is the Lord's solemn follow-up: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (John 5:14). The physical healing, great as it was, was not the man's deepest need; a worse thing than thirty-eight years of infirmity awaited the unrepentant — the eternal judgment of sin. The Lord who healed his body warned him to turn from sin, lest a worse thing come. Bethesda thus teaches that Christ's temporal mercies are meant to lead to repentance, and that the soul not turned from sin faces a worse calamity than any bodily affliction. The house of mercy issues a call to holiness: made whole, sin no more.

etymology: Greek Kenchreai; the eastern seaport of Corinth, on the Saronic Gulf, serving Corinth's trade toward Asia. The site of a church and the home of Phoebe the deaconess.
biblical_def: Cenchrea was the eastern harbor of Corinth, a port town on the Saronic Gulf, notable in the New Testament for being the home of a church, the place where the Apostle Paul fulfilled a vow, and the residence of Phoebe, the woman commended to the Romans as a servant of the church there. After his long ministry at Corinth, Paul departed by way of Cenchrea on his return toward Syria; Luke records, "having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow" (Acts 18:18), a reference to a Nazarite-style vow Paul had taken, the shaving of the head marking its completion (cf. Num 6). This brief notice shows the apostle to the Gentiles, who taught that believers are free from the ceremonial law, nonetheless observing a personal vow with Jewish associations — a reminder that Christian liberty does not forbid such personal devotions, though it does not require them, and that Paul became "all things to all men" (1 Cor 9:22) without compromising the gospel. Most significantly, Cenchrea was the home church of Phoebe, whom Paul commends at the close of Romans: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also" (Rom 16:1-2). Phoebe, likely the bearer of the epistle to the Romans, is called a "servant" (Greek diakonos) of the Cenchrean church — honored for her service and her succor of many, including Paul himself. Cenchrea thus testifies to the spread of the gospel into the port towns and trade-centers of the Roman world, to the place of devoted women in the service (not the eldership) of the church, and to the warmth of Christian commendation and hospitality that bound the scattered churches together. From the harbor of Cenchrea the gospel and its letters traveled the sea-lanes of the empire, carried by faithful servants like Phoebe.

corruption_summary: Cenchrea is corrupted when Paul's vow is read as inconsistency with his gospel of liberty, when Phoebe's commendation is pressed to overturn the male eldership, or when the warmth of Christian hospitality it models is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Phoebe-and-the-eldership over-reading. Phoebe is called a "servant" (Greek diakonos) of the church at Cenchrea, and some press this to argue for women in the ordained teaching/governing offices of elder or (ordained, authoritative) deacon. The text honors Phoebe highly — as a servant, a succourer of many, likely the trusted bearer of the epistle to the Romans — but it does not place her in the teaching-and-ruling office that Scripture reserves to qualified men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7). The word diakonos is used broadly of servants and ministers of many kinds; Phoebe's commendation honors her real and valued service without establishing female eldership. The dictionary gladly honors Phoebe and the many women whose service has blessed the church, within the order Scripture sets — an order that exalts, not diminishes, the dignity of women's ministry, while reserving the eldership to men.

Cenchrea has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the model of Christian commendation and hospitality, and the honor given to faithful service. Paul commends Phoebe to the Roman church, asking them to receive her and assist her — the warm, practical network of welcome and aid that bound the scattered churches together (cf. 3 John 5-8). The early church moved on the sea-lanes of the empire carried by such commended servants; letters of commendation, hospitality to traveling believers, and mutual assistance were the sinews of the church's unity. Cenchrea, the harbor from which Phoebe likely carried the epistle to the Romans, reminds the church to honor faithful service and to practice the warm hospitality that receives and aids the Lord's servants.
roots_summary: The eastern seaport of Corinth, home of a church and of Phoebe the servant (diakonos) commended by Paul (Rom 16:1-2); where Paul completed a Nazarite-style vow (Acts 18:18); a witness to the gospel in the port towns and to women's service in the church.
